claims.text: The Muradiye Mosque was built in 1425–1426.
The study dates the Arabic copy of the vakfiye to 22 Shawwal 833 (14 July 1430) and compares it with an Ottoman Turkish translation from 1907.
The study counts 58 waqf income sources, 89 staff members, and 24 types of duty in the vakfiye.
The vakfiye described in the study provides two meals a day to people who are present, without distinction.
Clerks recorded goods in and out; storekeepers safeguarded supplies; kitchen staff prepared meals.
The study says two architects were responsible for maintaining or repairing the complex’s fountains.
claims.caveat: This general duty is not tied to a specific surviving fountain.

claims.text: The inventory identifies the Sıbyan Mektebi (madrasa) fountain at the west end as the complex’s only waqf fountain. It describes a pointed brick niche, a sawtooth frame, two cup niches, and a 1.30 × 0.43 m stone basin.
claims.caveat: The fountain photo in Drive has not been matched to this entry.

claims.text: The inventory describes a 17 × 17 m arcaded madrasa courtyard, 16 rooms, a teaching iwan, and an octagonal marble pool.
claims.caveat: Keep the historic plan separate from later changes and the current interior.

claims.text: A 2020 study says the courtyard was later covered and that the madrasa opened as a Quran and manuscript museum in 2019.
claims.caveat: This reports the use at the time of publication; confirm its current use.

claims.text: The study finds different student stipend amounts in the Arabic copy and Ottoman Turkish translation; its author suspects the translation is wrong.
claims.caveat: Do not present either amount as a settled figure.

claims.text: The inventory places the imaret about 20 m northeast of the mosque and gives dimensions of about 13 × 40 m. It records oven traces and grain and oil storage jars; nearby storehouses, a wood shed, flour store, and stable no longer survive.
claims.caveat: The publication reports restaurant use from the early 2000s; verify the current use with an official or on-site source.

claims.text: The inventory lists thirteen tombs in the Muradiye complex, dated from 1442 to 1573.
claims.caveat: This follows the publication’s own classification and count.

claims.text: The inventory says Şehzade Mustafa died in 1553, was first buried elsewhere, and was moved to this tomb after it was built in 1573. An inscription above the door describes its construction.
The inventory describes an octagonal tomb with reused marble from a Bursa palace, 16th-century İznik tiles, and fourteen windows.
The inventory identifies three of four sarcophagi; the fourth is unknown and only possibly belongs to Şehzade Orhan.
claims.caveat: Preserve “unknown” as a valid answer. Do not turn a possibility into a fact.

claims.text: The player encounters a fictional discrepancy in a store record.
claims.caveat: This is a story device, not a historical event.

spatial_context.name: Bathhouse
spatial_context.text: The publication places the bathhouse west of the madrasa. It is not a story task.

spatial_context.name: Madrasa
spatial_context.text: At the west end of the complex, with an octagonal courtyard pool. The photo clue appears in Scene 2.

spatial_context.name: West fountain
spatial_context.text: A pointed brick niche has two cup niches. Scene 3 asks players to inspect these details and speak with a witness.

spatial_context.name: Mosque
spatial_context.text: Built in 1425–1426. It helps explain the complex layout but is not evidence in this case.

spatial_context.name: Imaret
spatial_context.text: About 20 m northeast of the mosque, according to the publication. Scenes 4–5 compare the kitchen receipt and original ledger.
